extracted.intended_audience: brand marketers, PR professionals, social media managers, communications teams
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for how brands should prepare for, respond to, and recover from visible public relations and social media crises, illustrated with real-world examples and 'lessons learned.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for your most visible and feasible risks
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical approach to crisis communication management is to plan for your most visible and feasible risks, and develop clear processes and practices to handle the unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page acknowledges you cannot plan for every possible source of crisis; instead prioritize risks that are both likely to be visible to the public and feasible to prepare for. Develop standard processes and practices so teams can act quickly when surprises occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common causes of PR crises
rubrics_metrics.description: List of frequent root causes: supply chain issues impacting product availability; product flaws (including safety hazards like explosions); unfair treatment of employees; cultural insensitivity in marketing or advertising; valuing profit more than public health; toxic culture or leadership; dismal customer support; making false or misleading statements; unexpected portrayals (e.g., fictional TV episodes making a product seem unsafe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this catalogue as a risk inventory to assess exposure. Not exhaustive, but highlights varied sources—operational, cultural, ethical, and reputational—that can trigger visible crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand awareness (as an evaluation criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The biggest PR crisis examples occur when a brand is widely known. Global B2C brands that are household names face heightened risks when a scandal occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating potential impact, consider brand recognition and scale—well-known brands will attract more attention and therefore require more robust preparedness and response mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media forums (include social and traditional channels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate crises across media forums: social media crises and traditional media each matter. Social media crisis management requires a unique set of crisis management tools and a nimble approach to crisis communication management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both social listening and traditional media monitoring in plans. Response cadence and tone may differ by forum; social media often requires faster, more concise engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of best-practice and cautionary examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing crisis responses, compare both 'Best practice examples' and '(Not so) Best practice examples' to extract actionable lessons for marketers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study successful and failed responses to understand what to emulate or avoid. Concrete case studies (KFC, Samsung, Burger King vs. Bud Light, Volkswagen, Balenciaga) illustrate principles in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success metric: minimize financial and reputational damage; return to business-as-usual
rubrics_metrics.description: With the types of crises featured, success is simply getting through the crisis with minimal financial and reputational damage. Getting back to business-as-usual is the number one goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame objectives for crisis response around limiting reputational loss and financial harm and restoring normal operations. Use measurable indicators (sales, sentiment, media coverage) to gauge recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take accountability and offer a sincere apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Even for factors beyond your company’s control, taking accountability and offering a sincere apology is often the best path to redemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: KFC UK apologized in a sincere-yet-amusing way rather than deflecting blame to partners. Tone should match severity; avoid hollow or performative apologies. Where appropriate, combine apology with clear next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take corrective action and communicate improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking corrective steps to bounce back from a crisis will yield far greater outcomes if you bring customers along on the journey through regular communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Samsung conducted extensive testing, engaged third-party auditors, established advisory boards, and shared quality-assurance efforts with customers (airport booths, email campaigns). Communicate tangible improvements and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act fast — social media spreads rapidly
rubrics_metrics.description: Act fast! Social media is called 'viral' because it can spread so quickly. Immediate action can prevent escalation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Burger King deleted an insensitive tweet within hours and added an apology and explanation. Rapid acknowledgement, correction, or removal can limit reach; delay risks exponential amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make the situation worse — avoid poor defensive moves
rubrics_metrics.description: If there’s a golden rule for crisis management it would be: don’t make the situation worse! During a crisis, every action will be viewed critically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid evasive, dismissive, or blaming responses. Poor responses (vague apologies, finger-pointing) prolong negative attention and erode trust, as seen in several case studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitive cultural issues: don't casually fish for sales lift
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitive cultural issues are no place to casually fish for sales lift. Brands may express values, but without fortitude and commitment to stand by those values, you risk offending everyone when you backpedal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bud Light's sponsorship tied to a transgender influencer became a lightning rod; half-hearted or opportunistic engagement on cultural topics can trigger backlash. If engaging on values, be prepared to sustain and defend them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prolonged denials — owning up shortens negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Volkswagen’s denials only served to anger their customer base, and prolonged the negativity far longer than necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When clear evidence of wrongdoing or failure exists, prompt acknowledgement and remediation reduce long-term reputational harm. Prolonged denials invite regulatory scrutiny and media investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t publicly blame hired vendors/creatives — it undermines credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When you publicly blame people you’ve hired for your crisis, many will question the company’s decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Balenciaga pulled a campaign then announced legal action against those responsible for the set; the public viewed this skeptically. Internal accountability is appropriate, but external blaming can appear evasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social listening and crisis management tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis communication management tools (e.g., SentiOne Listen) let you act quickly to avoid a public relations crisis by connecting you with opinions, questions, and pain points of clients and prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize monitoring: track brand mentions, conduct trend analysis, configure alerts, and gather insights from reports. Integrate alerts into escalation processes so teams can respond rapidly and consistently.
